text:
Let's explore [[Identify equivalent fractions when presented as shapes or objects]] and clear up the idea that [[When shading fractions of shapes, believes the denominator always means the number of sections that are not shaded]].

We will use a [[Fraction wall]]! Look at equal-length rows for halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, eighths, and twelfths. Find your fraction, trace straight down, and name exact matches where top and bottom are multiplied or divided by the same number. Rows that don't match show why adding, subtracting, or changing one number breaks equivalence. Now, predict one more!
